question.prompt: Why does the poem repeatedly draw attention to sounds such as rope knocks, engines and a bell?

options.text: they show the bay is crowded with people
they provide exact instructions for fishing
they establish that the boats are damaged
They connect the speaker's listening with the grandfather's knowledge

question.explanation: The grandfather's knowledge is auditory, and the speaker counts knocks while listening. Repeated sounds make that comparison central to the speaker's developing understanding.

stimulus.title: Night at the jetty
stimulus.body:
The jetty combs the dark with wooden teeth.
A rope knocks twice against a sleeping boat.
Across the bay, a window holds its breath;
then someone draws a curtain on its light.

I came to see the boats return like stars,
each yellow lamp a promise moving home.
But now the tide has folded up the sand,
and all the fishing boats are tied and still.

My grandfather once knew them by their sounds:
the gruff old engine, and the bell that skipped.
I cannot name a single boat by ear.
I count the knocks until the rope falls quiet.

At last I turn. Behind me, in the dark,
the water keeps a language I am learning.

workedSolution: The grandfather's knowledge is auditory, and the speaker counts knocks while listening.
Repeated sounds make that comparison central to the speaker's developing understanding.

question.prompt: What is missing at the start of 'The missing label'?
question.explanation: The stone is present, but Mina says it had a label yesterday. The problem is its missing identification, not the loss of the object or the whole display.

stimulus.title: The missing label
stimulus.body:
'We cannot display it without a name,' said Otis, holding a smooth grey stone above the exhibition table.

'It had a label yesterday,' Mina replied. She checked the floor, then the empty packing tray. Their class collection opened in ten minutes.

Otis looked at the other stones. 'This one looks like the basalt. We can write basalt again.'

Mina shook her head. 'Looking similar is not the same as knowing. Put it beside the others with a question mark.'

stimulus.title: Two accounts of the same race
stimulus.body:
Account A: I watched from the finish line. The runners appeared around the bend together, and Mara crossed first by less than a shoe length. When I caught up, Mara was thanking Jules for showing her how to pace the middle lap during training. Jules laughed and said, 'Next time I shall keep that trick to myself.' Then both offered to help me pin my number on more securely.

These accounts were written by different students after the fictional race. Neither writer saw and heard everything that happened.
